It appears in Kurdish, Persian, Turkish, Jewish, Arab and Egyptian traditional music, and in some regions it is the only wind instrument. Regional differences developed: the Persian ney mostly has six holes, the Arab and Turkish ney seven; Arab playing uses no mouthpiece, while in Turkey a brass, horn or plastic mouthpiece is often put at the top to protect the body and improve the blowhole. Modern metal or plastic tubes also exist, and the pitch varies with region and fingering. In Romania, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan the same or a similar name can mean a panpipe or a transverse flute, of different construction.

The ney is an edge-blown flute among aerophones, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.111.1. The body is mostly hollow reed or giant reed, with five or six fingerholes and a thumbhole; the Arab instrument has no mouthpiece, while the Turkish one can have a brass, horn or plastic mouthpiece at the top. It is used in Kurdish, Persian, Turkish, Jewish, Arab and Egyptian traditional music, and in some regions it is the only wind instrument. A skilled player can sound more than three octaves, and neys of different registers are usually kept to suit different modes.
